decks.title: Equality, Part 1: Meaning, Dimensions and Perspectives
goals: Explain why equality matters and give its standard definition
Distinguish justified from unjust differences, and natural from socially produced inequalities
Describe political, social and economic equality with imagined examples
Outline the perspectives of Lohia, Marxism, liberalism and feminism
Plan a five mark answer on the dimensions of equality

slides.heading: Equality: Meaning, Dimensions and Perspectives
slides.body_md: Part 1: why **equality** matters, what it means, its **dimensions** and the main **perspectives**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: why equality matters, what it means, natural and social inequalities, the three dimensions and the perspectives
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Equality is one of the great ideals of politics. In this part we ask why it matters and what it means. We separate natural from social inequalities, study the three dimensions of equality, and then look at four ways of thinking about it.

slides.heading: Why equality matters

rows: Equality is a powerful ideal: it holds that every person has the same worth
Its slogan joined liberty, equality and fraternity
Anti-colonial movements and movements against discrimination appealed to equality
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) is one international statement of equal worth and rights

visual.alt: Table on why equality matters: it is a powerful moral and political ideal; the French Revolution of 1789 joined liberty, equality and fraternity; anti-colonial movements and movements against discrimination appealed to equality; the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 is one international statement of equal worth and rights

slides.narration: Equality is a powerful moral and political ideal. It holds that every person has the same worth. The French Revolution joined liberty, equality and fraternity in its slogan. Movements against colonial rule and against discrimination appealed to it. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of nineteen forty eight is one international statement of it.

slides.heading: What equality means

rows: Every person counts as worthy of respect and consideration
Every visitor to the Ostrel library is greeted alike
No person is shut out of rights or chances to develop because of birth or status
Any child in Lindor may sit the school entrance test
Treatment may differ where a relevant ground such as need or work done justifies it
A clinic charges nothing to those who cannot pay
All persons deserve equal respect and consideration, equal rights, and equal opportunities to develop themselves

visual.alt: Table on the meaning of equality: equal respect, with the example of every visitor to the imagined Ostrel library greeted alike; equal rights and opportunities, with the example of any child in imagined Lindor sitting the entrance test; not identical treatment, since a relevant ground such as need or work can justify a difference, as when a clinic charges nothing to those who cannot pay; and the standard definition that all persons deserve equal respect and consideration, equal rights, and equal opportunities to develop themselves
visual.caption: Ostrel, Lindor and the clinic are imagined.

slides.narration: Equality means equal respect for all persons, with equal rights and equal opportunities. It does not mean identical treatment in every case. The standard definition is that all persons deserve equal respect and consideration, equal rights, and equal opportunities to develop themselves. An imagined clinic that charges nothing to those who cannot pay still respects this idea.

slides.heading: Justified and unjust differences

rows: A free lunch for children whose families cannot pay
A harvest bonus for those who worked extra hours
A rule that seats children of one caste at the back of the hall
Lower pay for women doing the same work as men

visual.alt: Table of justified and unjust differences in treatment: justified on the ground of need, as with a free lunch for children whose families cannot pay; justified on the ground of work done, as with a harvest bonus for extra hours; unjust on the ground of birth or status, as with seating children of one caste at the back of the hall; and unjust on the ground of sex alone, as with lower pay for women doing the same work as men; all examples are in imagined Quillby
visual.caption: Quillby and its people are imagined.

slides.narration: Some differences in treatment are justified. A free lunch for children who cannot pay rests on need. A harvest bonus rests on work done. Other differences are unjust, because they rest on birth, status or sex alone. Imagined Quillby shows both kinds. The test is whether the ground is relevant and respects every person.

Natural inequalities are differences of talent and ability, not made by social arrangements; imagined example, Tara sings better than her brother, who is quicker at chess; they are not a ground for unequal rights. Socially produced inequalities are made by social arrangements such as caste, class and gender discrimination; imagined example, a custom keeps girls of one hamlet out of school; they can be changed by society. A test to apply: ask whether society could have arranged things differently; if yes, the inequality is socially produced, and if no, it is natural
visual.caption: Natural and socially produced inequalities compared.

slides.narration: Natural inequalities are differences of talent and ability. Socially produced inequalities come from social arrangements, such as caste, class or gender discrimination. A helpful test is to ask whether society could have arranged things differently. If it could, the inequality is socially produced. A natural difference gives no ground for unequal rights.

slides.heading: The three dimensions of equality

rows: Equal citizenship, equal voting rights and civil rights
Every adult in Veldmoor has one equal vote
Equal opportunities, access to education and health care, and the removal of discrimination
Every child in Lindor may use the school and the clinic
Reducing large gaps in wealth and income
Quillby shares farmland more widely among families

slides.narration: Equality has three dimensions. Political equality covers equal citizenship, equal voting rights and civil rights. Social equality covers equal opportunities, access to education and health care, and the removal of discrimination. Economic equality covers reducing large gaps in wealth and income. Each has an imagined example.

visual.alt: Table on Ram Manohar Lohia: a thinker and political leader of the twentieth century; he held that inequality takes several kinds and each needs attention; the kinds he named are between men and women, by skin colour, by caste, colonial rule of some peoples over others, and economic inequality; the list shows that inequality has many sources, not only wealth

slides.narration: Ram Manohar Lohia was a thinker and political leader of the twentieth century. He held that inequality takes several kinds. He named inequality between men and women, by skin colour, by caste, colonial rule of some peoples over others, and economic inequality. The list shows that inequality has many sources, not only wealth.

slides.heading: Marxism and liberalism

rows: Rooted in the private ownership of resources
How resources are owned and shared
Competition is fair if opportunities are equal
Equal opportunities and wariness of concentrated power

visual.alt: Table comparing Marxism and liberalism: Marxism finds inequality rooted in the private ownership of resources and stresses how resources are owned and shared; liberalism holds competition to be fair if opportunities are equal and stresses equal opportunities and wariness of concentrated power

slides.narration: Marxism sees inequality as rooted in the private ownership of resources, and so looks at how resources are owned and shared. Liberalism accepts competition as fair if opportunities are equal, and is wary of concentrated power. The two views start from different concerns, and each gives reasons for its account.

rows: Equal rights for women and men

In Hesk, a group campaigns for daughters to inherit family land on the same terms as sons

slides.narration: Feminism works for equal rights for women and men. It challenges patriarchy, a social system in which men hold the dominant power in family and society. In imagined Hesk, a group campaigns for daughters to inherit land on the same terms as sons. Inequality between men and women is also one of the kinds that Lohia named.

slides.narration: To sum up. Equality is a powerful ideal that means equal respect, rights and opportunities, not identical treatment. Differences based on need or work can be justified, while those based on birth or status are unjust. Inequalities may be natural or socially produced. Equality has political, social and economic dimensions, and Lohia, Marxism, liberalism and feminism each give an account of it.

sections.heading: 1. Why equality matters and what it means
sections.body_md:
**Equality** is a powerful moral and political ideal: it treats every person as having the same worth. It inspired the **French Revolution** (1789), whose slogan joined liberty, equality and fraternity, and it inspired anti-colonial movements and movements against discrimination. The **Universal Declaration of Human Rights** (1948) is one international statement of equal worth and rights.

The standard definition: equality is the principle that all persons deserve **equal respect and consideration**, **equal rights** and **equal opportunities to develop themselves**. It does not call for identical treatment in every case.

key_terms.definition_md: The principle that all persons deserve equal respect and consideration, equal rights, and equal opportunities to develop themselves.
The same chance for every person to develop talents and take part in society, whatever the circumstances of birth.

Its slogan joined liberty, equality and fraternity
Anti-colonial movements and movements against discrimination appealed to equality
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) is one international statement of equal worth and rights

sections.heading: 2. Justified and unjust differences; natural and social inequalities
sections.body_md:
A difference in treatment is **justified** when it rests on a relevant ground, such as **need** or **work done**. It is **unjust** when it rests on **birth or status**, such as caste or sex.

**Natural inequalities** are differences of talent and ability. **Socially produced inequalities** come from social arrangements such as **caste, class or gender discrimination**. A natural difference gives no ground for unequal rights, while a social arrangement can be changed.

A difference between persons that arises from social arrangements, such as caste, class or gender discrimination.

sections.heading: 3. The three dimensions of equality
sections.body_md:
**Political equality** covers equal citizenship, equal voting rights and civil rights. **Social equality** covers equal opportunities, access to education and health care, and the removal of discrimination. **Economic equality** covers the reduction of large gaps in wealth and income.

The dimensions are linked: a person with a vote but no access to school or work may find it hard to use that vote well.

key_terms.definition_md: Equal citizenship, with equal voting rights and civil rights for all.
Equal opportunities, access to education and health care, and the removal of discrimination.
The reduction of large gaps in wealth and income.

sections.heading: 4. Perspectives on equality
sections.body_md:
**Ram Manohar Lohia** spoke of several kinds of inequality: between men and women, by skin colour, by caste, colonial rule of some peoples over others, and economic inequality.

**Marxism** sees inequality as rooted in the **private ownership of resources**. **Liberalism** accepts **competition** as fair if opportunities are equal, and is wary of concentrated power. **Feminism** works for **equal rights for women and men** and challenges **patriarchy**.

Each view gives its own account of the roots of inequality and of what to do about it; a student may weigh them with reasons.

A social system in which men hold the dominant power in family and society.

sections.heading: 5. Promoting equality: formal equality and differential treatment
sections.body_md:
**Formal equality** removes legal privileges and discrimination. In the Constitution, **Article 14** provides equality before the law and equal protection of the laws; **Article 15** forbids discrimination on grounds such as religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; **Article 17** abolishes untouchability. Article 15(3) allows special provisions for women and children.

Formal equality may leave real inequalities in place. **Differential treatment** gives special arrangements, such as **ramps** for persons with disabilities and **maternity benefits**, so that persons can enjoy equal access.

key_terms.definition_md: The removal of legal privileges and discrimination, so that the law treats all persons alike.
A special arrangement for persons in different circumstances so that they have an equal chance to enjoy the same rights and services.

sections.heading: 6. Affirmative action and the debate on reservations
sections.body_md:
**Affirmative action** means policies that aim to remedy the effects of historical disadvantage. In India it takes the form of **reservations** in education and public jobs for **Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes**, permitted by **Article 15(4)** and **Article 16(4)**.

The debate: **some argue** that reservations correct long-standing disadvantage and make institutions representative. **Others argue** for other or additional means, such as scholarships, coaching or hostels, or for different criteria. Students may weigh both sets of reasons and judge for themselves.

A dated fact (as of 2024): the **103rd Amendment (2019)** added reservation for economically weaker sections, and the Supreme Court upheld it in 2022.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying equality means identical treatment: it means equal respect, rights and opportunities, and some differences are justified.
- Mixing natural and social inequalities: natural differences are of talent and ability; social ones are made by arrangements that can be changed.
- Ranking the perspectives: state each view with its reason and leave the judgement to the reader.
- Mixing up the Articles: 14 equality before the law, 15 no discrimination, 17 untouchability abolished, 15(4) and 16(4) special provision and reservation.
- Taking a side on reservations: write some argue, others argue, and give reasons for each.
- Leaving out the date: write the 103rd Amendment (2019), upheld in 2022, as of 2024.

**Tips:** give a short imagined example with each definition; add a one-line link between the three dimensions; end a debate answer by saying that students may weigh the reasons and judge.

Equal rights for women and men, challenging patriarchy.
A social system in which men hold the dominant power in family and society.

Equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws.
Discrimination on grounds such as religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
Abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice.

cards.front_md: Which groups benefit from reservations in India?
cards.back_md: Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes.
Special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
Reservation in public appointments for backward classes not adequately represented.

cards.front_md: One reason **others argue** for other or additional means
cards.back_md: Scholarships, coaching or hostels, or different criteria, may help more children.

questions.stem_md: Which slogan, linked with the French Revolution of 1789, placed equality beside two other ideals?

options.text_md: Order, tradition and obedience
Liberty, equality and fraternity
Wealth, power and honour
Peace, trade and empire

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Liberty, equality and fraternity. Equality stood with liberty and fraternity in the revolutionary slogan. The other three sets of words do not make up that slogan.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best captures what equality means in political theory?

options.text_md: Giving every person exactly the same income and the same job
Treating every difference between persons as unjust
Removing all differences of talent between persons
Equal respect for all persons, with equal rights and opportunities, though not identical treatment in every case

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Equal respect for all persons, with equal rights and opportunities, though not identical treatment in every case. Equality is about equal respect, rights and opportunities. It does not demand the same income, the same job or the removal of every difference, since some differences in treatment are justified.

questions.stem_md: Which statement gives the standard definition of equality?

options.text_md: All persons deserve equal respect and consideration, equal rights, and equal opportunities to develop themselves
All persons must receive the same reward for every kind of work
Only citizens of one region deserve equal rights
The rich and the poor must live in the same houses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** All persons deserve equal respect and consideration, equal rights, and equal opportunities to develop themselves. The standard definition joins equal respect, equal rights and equal opportunities to develop. The other options ask for identical rewards or homes, or confine rights to one region.

questions.stem_md: What are natural inequalities?

options.text_md: Differences created by caste and class systems
Differences created by unequal laws
Differences between people in talents, abilities and similar qualities
Differences created by large gaps in wealth

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Differences between people in talents, abilities and similar qualities. Natural inequalities are differences of talent and ability. Caste, class, unequal laws and large wealth gaps are social arrangements, so they are socially produced inequalities.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined village of Quillby, Tara sings far better than her brother Joel, while Joel solves chess puzzles faster than Tara. How should these two differences be classed?

options.text_md: As socially produced inequalities, since the village made them
As unjust discrimination by the village
As natural inequalities of talent, which do not by themselves justify unequal rights
As economic inequalities in wealth

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** As natural inequalities of talent, which do not by themselves justify unequal rights. Differences in singing and puzzle-solving are differences of ability, so they are natural inequalities. No social arrangement made them, and they give no ground for giving Tara and Joel unequal rights.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Brindle Hill Club of Ostrel admits as members only men from families that have lived in the town for three generations. The difference between those admitted and those refused is best described as

options.text_md: a socially produced inequality based on sex and birth, with no justification of need or work
a natural inequality of talent
a difference justified by the work members do
a difference that follows from need alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a socially produced inequality based on sex and birth, with no justification of need or work. Sex and family origin are not measures of need or work, and the rule is a social arrangement. It is therefore a socially produced inequality. Talent, work and need are not the basis of the rule.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Lindor health centre treats every patient but charges nothing to patients who cannot pay and a small fee to those who can. Which view of this difference in charges is sound?

options.text_md: It is unjust because it treats patients differently
It is unjust because the centre should charge everyone a high fee
It is justified only if the poor are refused treatment
It can be justified by need and is not discrimination based on birth or status

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** It can be justified by need and is not discrimination based on birth or status. Equality allows differences in treatment that rest on a relevant ground such as need. The charge depends on ability to pay and not on caste, sex or birth. Refusing treatment to the poor, or a high uniform fee, would not fit equal respect.

questions.stem_md: Marrowdale Foods Ltd, an imagined company, pays women packers less than men packers for exactly the same work and hours. This is best described as

options.text_md: a justified difference based on work done
an unjust difference based on sex, which fails the test of equal respect
a natural inequality of strength
a difference justified by need

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** an unjust difference based on sex, which fails the test of equal respect. The work and hours are the same, so the pay gap rests on sex and not on work done or need. It is an unjust difference. Natural inequality of strength is not shown by the case.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following belongs to political equality?

options.text_md: Equal citizenship, with equal voting rights and civil rights
Equal wealth for every household
Equal marks for every student
Equal talents for every person

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Equal citizenship, with equal voting rights and civil rights. Political equality covers equal citizenship, voting rights and civil rights. Equal wealth is an economic matter, while equal marks and talents are neither a dimension of equality nor an aim of it.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined village of Lindor, children of one caste are not allowed to use the village library, and they are the only children without a school nearby. Which dimension of equality is mainly in question?

options.text_md: Political equality, which covers voting
Social equality, which covers equal opportunities and the removal of discrimination
Economic equality, which covers only gaps in income
Natural equality of talent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Social equality, which covers equal opportunities and the removal of discrimination. Exclusion from a library and a school on the ground of caste concerns opportunities and discrimination, which is social equality. Voting and income gaps are not what the case describes.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined district of Quillby, the richest tenth of families own most of the farmland and earn many times more than the rest. Proposals to reduce this gap by sharing resources more widely address mainly

options.text_md: political equality
natural equality
economic equality
formal equality of citizenship

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** economic equality. A large gap in wealth and income is an economic inequality, and narrowing it is the concern of economic equality. Voting rights, talents and legal status are not the matter here.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined town of Veldmoor, votes cast in the hill wards are counted as half a vote each, while votes in the river wards count in full. Which dimension of equality does this rule violate?

options.text_md: Economic equality, since income differs
Natural equality of talent
Social equality in the use of wells
Political equality, since equal voting rights are denied

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Political equality, since equal voting rights are denied. Counting some citizens' votes at half value breaks equal voting rights, which belong to political equality. The rule is about votes, not income, talent or wells.

questions.stem_md: Ram Manohar Lohia spoke of several kinds of inequality. Which set lists kinds he named?

options.text_md: Between languages, between sports, by height and by age only
Between towns and villages, by hobby and by dress only
Between rivers, mountains and plains
Between men and women, by skin colour, by caste, colonial rule and economic inequality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Between men and women, by skin colour, by caste, colonial rule and economic inequality. Lohia named inequality between men and women, by skin colour, by caste, colonial rule over some peoples by others, and economic inequality. The other sets are not among the kinds he spoke of.

questions.stem_md: According to Marxism, where is inequality rooted?

options.text_md: In differences of natural talent
In competition between equal persons
In the private ownership of resources
In the absence of any rules

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** In the private ownership of resources. Marxism traces inequality to private ownership of resources. Natural talent, competition among persons with equal opportunities and the absence of rules are not its account.

questions.stem_md: At a debate in Ostrel, a speaker says that a running race is fair when all runners start from the same line with the same chance, and that the winner may keep the prize. Which perspective does this speaker's approach most resemble?

options.text_md: Marxism, which roots inequality in private ownership
Liberalism, which accepts competition as fair if opportunities are equal
Feminism, which challenges patriarchy
None of them, since no perspective deals with fairness

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Liberalism, which accepts competition as fair if opportunities are equal. Accepting competition as fair when opportunities are equal is the liberal approach. The other two perspectives start from other concerns, namely ownership of resources and patriarchy, and fairness is a concern of all.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined community of Hesk, custom lets only sons inherit family land. A group campaigns for daughters to inherit equally, calling the custom a form of patriarchy. Which perspective on equality does the group represent?

options.text_md: Feminism, which works for equal rights for women and men
Liberalism, which defends competition only
Marxism, which looks only at class
Colonial rule, a kind of inequality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Feminism, which works for equal rights for women and men. Working for equal inheritance rights for women and challenging patriarchy is the feminist perspective. Liberalism and Marxism have other starting points, and colonial rule is a kind of inequality, not a perspective.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the perspectives on equality is accurate?

options.text_md: Marxism accepts competition as always fair, while liberalism blames private ownership
Marxism stresses private ownership of resources, while liberalism accepts competition when opportunities are equal
Feminism holds that patriarchy is not a cause of inequality
All four views name the same single cause of inequality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Marxism stresses private ownership of resources, while liberalism accepts competition when opportunities are equal. The first statement matches the two accounts. The second swaps them. Feminism challenges patriarchy as a source of inequality. The four views do not name one single cause.

questions.stem_md: What is formal equality?

options.text_md: The sharing of all wealth equally
Special seats set aside in colleges
Equal talents for all
The removal of legal privileges and of discrimination in law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The removal of legal privileges and of discrimination in law. Formal equality means ending legal privileges and legal discrimination. Sharing wealth, special seats and equal talents are other matters.

questions.stem_md: Which Article of the Constitution abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice?

options.text_md: Article 17
Article 14
Article 15(4)
Article 16(4)

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Article 17. Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Article 14 speaks of equality before law, and Articles 15(4) and 16(4) deal with special provisions and reservation.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined state of Veldmoor, a rule says that relatives of ministers need not obey the traffic laws that bind everyone else. Which constitutional idea does this rule go against?

options.text_md: The abolition of untouchability, the idea of Article 17
Special provisions for backward classes, the idea of Article 15(4)
Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws, the idea of Article 14
The idea of Article 16(4) alone, since it concerns public jobs only

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Equality before the law and equal protection of the laws, the idea of Article 14. Giving a privilege before the law to one group goes against the equality before law that Article 14 provides. Article 17 is about untouchability, Article 15(4) allows special provisions and Article 16(4) concerns jobs.

questions.stem_md: The only tea shop in the imagined town of Ostrel refuses to serve customers of one caste. Which Article's guarantee against discrimination does this practice go against?

options.text_md: Article 16(4), which allows reservation in appointments
Article 15(4), which allows special provisions for backward classes
Article 15, which forbids discrimination on grounds such as caste in access to shops and public places
No Article, since a tea shop is a private matter

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Article 15, which forbids discrimination on grounds such as caste in access to shops and public places. Article 15 forbids discrimination on grounds such as religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, and covers access to shops, restaurants and similar places. Articles 15(4) and 16(4) allow special provisions and do not permit such refusal.

questions.stem_md: Why can special treatment for some persons sometimes help achieve real equality?

options.text_md: Because persons differ in their circumstances, and equal access may need special arrangements
Because equality means treating no one alike
Because special treatment ends all differences
Because it replaces the need for any law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Because persons differ in their circumstances, and equal access may need special arrangements. Persons start from different circumstances, so the same arrangement may leave some unable to use it. Special treatment such as a ramp creates equal access. It does not mean treating no one alike, ending all differences or replacing law.

questions.stem_md: The imagined Ostrel hospital gives paid leave to mothers after childbirth and fits a ramp at its main door for wheelchair users. How should these steps be described?

options.text_md: Formal equality alone
Affirmative action for a historically disadvantaged community
Discrimination against fathers and walkers
Equality through differential treatment, since special provision helps real equality

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Equality through differential treatment, since special provision helps real equality. Maternity leave and a ramp are special provisions that make equal use of work and buildings possible, which is differential treatment. They are not about legal privilege, historical disadvantage of a community or unjust discrimination.

questions.stem_md: What is affirmative action?

options.text_md: Laws that remove all differences in income
Policies that aim to remedy the effects of historical disadvantage
A rule that every institution must treat all applicants identically
The ending of all special provisions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Policies that aim to remedy the effects of historical disadvantage. Affirmative action means policies that remedy the effects of historical disadvantage. Removing all income differences, identical treatment in all cases and ending special provisions describe other things.

questions.stem_md: Articles 15(4) and 16(4) of the Constitution are the basis for which kind of policy?

options.text_md: Special provision and reservation in education and public jobs for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes
Voting rights for all adults
The abolition of untouchability
Freedom of speech

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Special provision and reservation in education and public jobs for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes. These two Articles permit special provisions in education and reservation in public appointments for backward groups. Voting rights, abolition of untouchability and freedom of speech come under other provisions.

questions.stem_md: Hesk Polytechnic, an imagined college, sets aside 20 of its 100 seats for applicants from families that have lacked schooling for generations. Which description fits this step best?

options.text_md: A measure of formal equality only
An affirmative action policy aimed at remedying historical disadvantage
A removal of all differences of talent
A measure aimed solely at wealth and income

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** An affirmative action policy aimed at remedying historical disadvantage. Setting aside seats for families long denied schooling is an affirmative action policy. Formal equality is about removing legal privilege, talent differences are natural, and the step is not aimed at wealth alone.

questions.stem_md: At a school debate in Lindor, a student says that seats alone do not help a child who cannot afford books, so scholarships, coaching classes and hostels should be given as well or instead. How should this view be described?

options.text_md: A claim that equality does not matter
A view that opposes every public policy
A view that favours other or additional means to promote equality
A proof that the other side is wrong

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A view that favours other or additional means to promote equality. The student proposes other or additional measures to promote equality, which is one side of the debate. The student does not say equality is unimportant or oppose all policies, and the point does not settle the debate.

questions.stem_md: Which is an argument offered in support of reservations?

options.text_md: They remove the need for any school
They make all talents equal
They end all competition for jobs
They help correct long-standing disadvantage and make institutions more representative

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** They help correct long-standing disadvantage and make institutions more representative. Supporters argue that reservations correct long-standing disadvantage and make institutions representative. They do not remove the need for schools, make talents equal or end competition.

questions.stem_md: As of 2024, what did the 103rd Amendment (2019) add?

options.text_md: The abolition of untouchability
The right to vote for all adults
The equal protection of the laws
Reservation for economically weaker sections, upheld by the Supreme Court in 2022

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Reservation for economically weaker sections, upheld by the Supreme Court in 2022. The 103rd Amendment of 2019 added reservation for economically weaker sections, and the Supreme Court upheld it in 2022. Untouchability, adult voting and equal protection of laws come from other provisions.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Two sisters in Quillby differ in running speed, and the difference is a natural inequality.

**Reason (R):** Natural inequalities arise from differences in talent and ability and not from social arrangements.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true and R is true. Running speed is a difference of ability, and R states why such a difference counts as natural, so R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Equality requires that every person be treated in an identical way in every situation.

**Reason (R):** Persons differ in their needs and circumstances, so identical treatment can sometimes leave a disadvantage in place.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false, since equality asks for equal respect, rights and opportunities, not identical treatment everywhere. R is true and shows why A fails.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Equal citizenship, including an equal vote, belongs to political equality.

**Reason (R):** Large gaps in wealth and income are an economic inequality.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true. But the gap in wealth belongs to another dimension and does not explain why citizenship and the vote belong to the political one.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Formal equality alone may leave real inequalities in place.

**Reason (R):** Removing legal privileges does not, by itself, give a poor child a school that she can reach.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A is true and R is true. R gives an example of a real inequality that remains after legal privilege is removed, so it explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Affirmative action is meant to remedy the effects of historical disadvantage.

**Reason (R):** Affirmative action is meant to place one community above all others for ever.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true, since remedying historical disadvantage is its stated aim. R is false, because its aim is to correct disadvantage, not to rank a community above others.

questions.stem_md: A canteen in Veldmoor serves larger portions to the labourers who lift sacks all day than to the clerks. This proves that equality is always violated when treatment differs.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A difference in portions rests on work done and need, which are relevant grounds. Equality is violated by differences based on birth or status, not by every difference in treatment.

questions.stem_md: A difference in talent for music between two students is a natural inequality, but keeping girls out of the village school by custom is a socially produced inequality.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Talent is a natural difference. Exclusion by custom is a social arrangement, which can be changed, so it is socially produced.

questions.stem_md: Reservations in education and public jobs for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes rest on Article 17, which abolishes untouchability.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Reservations are permitted by Article 15(4) for education and Article 16(4) for public appointments.

questions.stem_md: Equal voting rights belong to ___ equality, while reducing large gaps in wealth and income belongs to ___ equality.
questions.solution_md: Equal voting rights are part of political equality, and reducing large gaps in wealth and income is part of economic equality.

questions.stem_md: The removal of legal privileges and discrimination is called ___ equality, and a ramp for wheelchair users is an example of ___ treatment.
questions.solution_md: Removing legal privileges and discrimination is formal equality, and a ramp is an example of differential treatment, meaning special provision for real equality.

questions.stem_md: Article ___ abolishes untouchability, and Article ___ provides for equality before the law.
questions.solution_md: Article 17 abolishes untouchability, and Article 14 provides for equality before the law.

questions.stem_md: Match each perspective on equality with the idea it stresses.

options.text_md: Marxism
Liberalism
Feminism
Lohia

match_right.text_md: Competition is fair if opportunities are equal
Several kinds of inequality, including caste and colonial rule
Inequality is rooted in the private ownership of resources
Equal rights for women and men; challenge to patriarchy

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Marxism is paired with private ownership of resources, liberalism with fair competition under equal opportunities, feminism with equal rights and a challenge to patriarchy, and Lohia with several kinds of inequality.

questions.stem_md: Match each provision of the Constitution with what it provides.

options.text_md: Article 14
Article 15(4)
Article 16(4)
Article 17

match_right.text_md: Reservation in public appointments for backward classes
Special provisions for backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Article 14 is equality before law, Article 15(4) is special provisions for backward groups, Article 16(4) is reservation in appointments, and Article 17 is the abolition of untouchability.

questions.stem_md: The imagined council of Ostrel wants to check whether a difference in treatment at the town pool is justified. Arrange its steps of reasoning in a sensible order.

options.text_md: Decide whether the difference is justified or unjust
Ask what the ground of the difference is: need, work done, or birth and status
Test whether the ground is relevant to the service and respects equal respect for all
Identify exactly how two groups are treated differently

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The council first states the difference, then finds its ground, then tests whether the ground is relevant and respectful, and only then decides.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange these ways of promoting equality in the order in which they widen from the basic to the most targeted.

options.text_md: Affirmative action: policies to remedy historical disadvantage
Differential treatment: special arrangements such as ramps and maternity benefits
Formal equality: remove legal privileges and discrimination

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (b) → (a). The ladder begins with formal equality, moves to special arrangements that help real equality, and reaches affirmative action, which targets historical disadvantage.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Define equality, and say why it does not require identical treatment in every case.
questions.solution_md: Definition and the note on justified differences.

answer.model_answer_md: **Equality** is the principle that all persons deserve equal respect and consideration, equal rights and equal opportunities to develop themselves. It does not demand identical treatment, because differences based on relevant grounds such as need or work done can be justified.

marking_scheme.step: Justified differences mean treatment need not be identical

questions.stem_md: Distinguish natural inequalities from socially produced inequalities, with one imagined example of each.
questions.solution_md: Both kinds defined, with examples.

answer.model_answer_md: **Natural inequalities** are differences of talent and ability, such as a gift for music. **Socially produced inequalities** arise from social arrangements, such as caste, class or gender discrimination, for example a village custom that keeps girls from school.

marking_scheme.step: Natural inequality defined, with an example
Socially produced inequality defined, with an example

questions.stem_md: Marrowdale Foods Ltd, an imagined company, pays a night-shift allowance to staff who work after midnight. Is this an unjust difference in pay? Give a reason.
questions.solution_md: Work done is a relevant ground.

answer.model_answer_md: No. The allowance rests on **work done**, since night work is harder, and not on birth, sex or status. A difference based on a relevant ground can be justified and does not fail the test of **equal respect**.

marking_scheme.step: A relevant ground, work done, is named
The difference does not rest on birth or status, so equal respect is kept

questions.stem_md: Name the three dimensions of equality and give one aspect of each.
questions.solution_md: Three dimensions, one aspect each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Political equality**: equal citizenship, including equal voting rights. **Social equality**: equal opportunities, such as access to education and health care. **Economic equality**: reducing large gaps in wealth and income.

questions.stem_md: State, in neutral terms, how Marxism and liberalism each look at inequality.
questions.solution_md: Each view stated.

answer.model_answer_md: In **Marxism**, inequality is traced to the private ownership of resources. **Liberalism** accepts competition as fair when opportunities are equal, and is wary of concentrated power. The two views start from different concerns.

marking_scheme.step: Liberalism: competition fair if opportunities are equal

questions.stem_md: Which kinds of inequality did Ram Manohar Lohia speak of?
questions.solution_md: Five kinds listed.

answer.model_answer_md: Lohia spoke of several kinds of inequality: between **men and women**, by **skin colour**, by **caste**, between peoples through **colonial rule**, and **economic** inequality.

questions.stem_md: What is formal equality? Name one Article that expresses it.
questions.solution_md: Definition and an Article.

answer.model_answer_md: **Formal equality** is the ending of legal privilege and discrimination, with the law treating everyone alike. **Article 14**, which provides equality before the law, is one expression of it, as is Article 17, which abolishes untouchability.

marking_scheme.step: Removal of legal privileges and discrimination
An Article named with its provision

questions.stem_md: Why may differential treatment be needed to achieve real equality? Give an imagined example.
questions.solution_md: Reason and example.

answer.model_answer_md: Persons start from different circumstances, so the same arrangement may not give each an equal chance. For example, the imagined Ostrel library builds a **ramp** so that wheelchair users can enter. This **special arrangement** gives them equal access.

marking_scheme.step: Circumstances differ, so identical arrangements may not give equal access
An imagined example such as a ramp

questions.stem_md: What is affirmative action? Name two groups for whom reservations are provided in India.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and two groups.

answer.model_answer_md: **Affirmative action** means policies that remedy the effects of historical disadvantage. In India reservations in education and public jobs are provided for **Scheduled Castes**, **Scheduled Tribes** and **Other Backward Classes**.

questions.stem_md: Which Articles permit reservation in education and public jobs, and what does each allow?
questions.solution_md: Two Articles with their provisions.

answer.model_answer_md: **Article 15(4)** permits special provisions, including in education, for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. **Article 16(4)** permits reservation in public appointments for backward classes not adequately represented.

marking_scheme.step: Article 15(4): special provisions for backward groups

questions.stem_md: Explain political, social and economic equality, with one imagined example of each.
questions.solution_md: Each dimension with its example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Political equality** gives all citizens equal citizenship, voting rights and civil rights, as when every adult in imagined Veldmoor has one vote. **Social equality** means equal opportunities, access to education and health care and no discrimination, as when every child in Lindor may use the school. **Economic equality** means reducing large gaps in wealth and income.

marking_scheme.step: Economic equality with an example or explanation

questions.stem_md: Describe how Marxism, liberalism and feminism each approach equality.
questions.solution_md: Three approaches, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md: In **Marxism**, inequality is traced to the private ownership of resources. For **liberalism**, competition is fair provided opportunities are equal, and concentrated power is a worry. **Feminism** works for equal rights for women and men, and challenges patriarchy. Each offers its own account of where inequality comes from.

questions.stem_md: Three situations are imagined in Veldmoor: (i) Kiran can carry heavier loads than Lila; (ii) farm workers of one community are not allowed to draw water from the common well; (iii) Mohan has a gift for languages. questions.stem_md: Explain how formal equality, differential treatment and affirmative action differ in the way they promote equality.
questions.solution_md: Three approaches contrasted.

answer.model_answer_md: **Formal equality** removes legal privileges and discrimination, as in Articles 14, 15 and 17. **Differential treatment** gives special arrangements, such as ramps or maternity benefits, so that persons can enjoy equal access. **Affirmative action** is a policy to remedy historical disadvantage, as in reservations in education and jobs.

questions.stem_md: Explain what equality means, and distinguish justified differences from unjust ones and natural inequalities from socially produced ones.
questions.solution_md: Definition, justified and unjust differences, natural and social inequalities.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Equality** means that all persons deserve equal respect and consideration, equal rights and equal opportunities to develop themselves.
2. It does not require identical treatment in every case.
3. A difference in treatment can be **justified** when it rests on a relevant ground such as need or work done.
4. A difference is **unjust** when it rests on birth or status, such as caste or sex.
5. **Natural inequalities** are differences of talent and ability.
6. **Socially produced inequalities** come from social arrangements such as caste, class or gender discrimination, and can be changed.

marking_scheme.step: Equality does not mean identical treatment
Justified differences: need or work done

questions.stem_md: Explain the three dimensions of equality, giving an imagined example of each and showing how they are linked.
questions.solution_md: Three dimensions with examples and a link.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Political equality** means equal citizenship, equal voting rights and civil rights. Example: every adult in imagined Veldmoor casts one equal vote.
2. **Social equality** means equal opportunities, access to education and health care, and the removal of discrimination. Example: a clinic in Lindor open to every caste.
3. **Economic equality** means reducing large gaps in wealth and income. Example: sharing farmland more widely in Quillby.
4. The dimensions are **linked**: an equal vote means little to a person kept from school and work.

marking_scheme.step: The dimensions are linked, with a reason

questions.stem_md: Describe the perspectives of Ram Manohar Lohia, Marxism, liberalism and feminism on inequality. Present them neutrally.
questions.solution_md: Four perspectives, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Lohia** spoke of several kinds of inequality: between men and women, by skin colour, by caste, colonial rule, and economic inequality.
2. In **Marxism**, inequality is traced to the private ownership of resources.
3. For **liberalism**, competition is fair provided opportunities are equal, and concentrated power is a worry.
4. **Feminism** works for equal rights for women and men, and challenges patriarchy.
5. The four views differ in where they place the roots of inequality and in the remedies they stress. A student may weigh each with reasons.

marking_scheme.step: Lohia: several kinds of inequality named
Liberalism: competition fair if opportunities equal; wary of concentrated power
Feminism: equal rights; challenge to patriarchy

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways of promoting equality: formal equality, differential treatment and affirmative action.
questions.solution_md: Three approaches with Articles and examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Formal equality** ends legal privilege and legal discrimination.
2. In the Constitution, **Article 14** provides equality before the law, **Article 15** forbids discrimination on grounds such as caste and sex, and **Article 17** abolishes untouchability.
3. **Differential treatment** means special arrangements that help achieve real equality, for example ramps or maternity benefits.
4. **Affirmative action** means policies to remedy historical disadvantage, such as reservations in education and public jobs under Articles 15(4) and 16(4).
5. Formal equality alone may leave real inequalities, so the three approaches work together.

marking_scheme.step: Why formal equality alone may not be enough

questions.stem_md: Explain affirmative action in India and the debate on reservations. Present both views and let the reader judge.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, Articles, both views, neutral ending.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Affirmative action** means policies to remedy the effects of historical disadvantage.
2. In India it takes the form of **reservations** in education and public jobs for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Other Backward Classes, permitted by **Articles 15(4) and 16(4)**.
3. Some argue that reservations are needed to correct **long-standing disadvantage** and to make institutions **representative**.
4. Others favour **other or additional measures**, for example scholarships, coaching or hostels, or different criteria.
5. Each side gives reasons, and students may weigh them and judge for themselves.

marking_scheme.step: Reasons for other or additional means or different criteria
Neutral conclusion that leaves the judgement to the student

questions.stem_md: The imagined council of Quillby wants to widen opportunity. It considers (i) a law that bars discrimination in all shops, (ii) a ramp and a lift at its offices, and (iii) a scholarship scheme for children of groups long denied schooling. Classify each measure and say what each would achieve.
questions.solution_md: Each measure classified with its effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Measure (i) is **formal equality**: it removes discrimination in access to shops.
2. It protects equal treatment in law but does not by itself supply opportunity.
3. Measure (ii) is **differential treatment**: a special arrangement that gives persons with disabilities equal access.
4. Measure (iii) is **affirmative action**: a policy aimed at the effects of historical disadvantage.
5. Together the measures address legal, practical and historical barriers. Some may prefer one measure over another, and the council should weigh reasons.

marking_scheme.step: Measure (ii) classified as differential treatment with its effect
Measure (iii) classified as affirmative action with its effect
Balanced conclusion that reasons must be weighed
